newsitem.title: CHINA: HK's Tung to make first official trip to U.S.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung to make first official trip to U.S.

text.p: Hong Kong's new leader Tung Chee-hwa will make his first official visit to the United States next month to meet President Bill Clinton and to convince Americans that all is well under Chinese rule.

Tung, chosen by a China-appointed committee to run Hong Kong after Britain ended its colonial rule on June 30, will visit Washington and New York from September 9 to 11, the government said on Thursday.

It is likely the post-colonial leader would try to impress upon President Clinton and congressmen that "business is as usual" in Hong Kong after the takeover by communist China six weeks ago, an analyst said.

Concerns have been raised that civil and political liberties in Hong Kong would be curbed after Tung's government watered down human rights protection laws and a legislature handpicked by China replaced an elected council after July 1.
In April, Tung cancelled his plans for a pre-handover visit to the United States, saying he was too busy.

Analysts said the cancellation was probably to avoid embarrassment over the rolling back of civil liberties laws and the success of Hong Kong's pro-democracy advocate Martin Lee's meeting with President Clinton.
At the time, Lee dominated headlines about the territory as he toured Europe and North America, warning the West of China's planned curbs of democracy and freedom in Hong Kong.
Tung would also visit London and Brussels from October 19 to 23, the government said.
Meanwhile, the new chief of China's Hong Kong watchdog met Tung on Thursday and assured him the agency would not meddle in his government.
Jiang Enzhu, director of the Xinhua News Agency branch, told Tung during their first official meeting that his office would not interfere in the running of local affairs.

However, Jiang said the Xinhua office, the Chinese Communist Party's Hong Kong base, would continue to maintain contacts with Hong Kong people from all walks of life in order to improve ties, according to a government statement.

At the same time, the head of Hong Kong's administration, Chief Secretary Anson Chan, praised the head of China's new Foreign Ministry office in Hong Kong for honouring a pledge not to meddle in the territory's affairs.
Ma Yuzhen, the head representative in Hong Kong of China's Foreign Ministry, "has made it quite clear...that he would not interfere in the activities in Hong Kong," she told reporters.
"I can say, in practice, that he has done exactly that. He has not interfered...so I am delighted we are off to a good start with Mr Ma," she said.
Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule on July 1 after 156 years of British control and is now a special autonomous region with a high degree of autonomy, except in diplomacy and defence.
Ma's office handles Hong Kong's external affairs and serves as a channel to Beijing, while Xinhua will remain the Chinese Communist Party's base in Hong Kong.
Xinhua acted as a watchdog and shadow government in the colonial era. Its deputy directors were like shadow ministers tracking specific policy areas.
This role is likely to be greatly reduced now that Hong Kong is ruled by a China-backed government.
